    Breaking: The Other Summitry in Shenzhen

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.
    • The highlights this week: Three regional presidents travel to China, the United States and Venezuela strike a military deal, and the region weighs fossil fuel phaseout looks at COP31.
    • Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

    The highlights this week: Three regional presidents travel to China, the United States and Venezuela strike a military deal, and the region weighs fossil fuel phaseout looks at COP31.

    Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

    The highlights this week: Three regional presidents travel to China, the United States and Venezuela strike a military deal, and the region weighs fossil fuel phaseout plans at COP31.

    This week, many observers focused on the trilateral meeting among the presidents of China, Russia, and the United States on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Three Latin American presidents were also in Shenzhen, China, for the meetings: those of Chile, Mexico, and Peru.

    It has been revealed that all six countries are APEC members. Though the bloc’s Latin American leaders don’t always attend the annual summit in person, they did this year—and held separate bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The 2028 APEC conference, hosted by Mexico, will see Asian leaders travel to Latin America.

    In their trips to Shenzhen, the three presidents signaled that they value relations with China despite pressure from the United States to spurn the country.

    The U.S. National Security Strategy issued by the Trump administration last year noted that allowing “non-Hemispheric competitors” to grow their presence in the Americas was a “strategic mistake.” And the U.S. ambassadors to both Mexico and Peru disparaged China in social media posts this week.

    According to recent reports, mexico has applied new tariffs on Chinese goods since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office, with some as high as 50 percent. But China remains Mexico’s No. 2 trade partner, and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said in Shenzhen that she hoped her trip would yield more Mexican avocado and tequila exports to China and new cooperation on smart hospitals.

    For Mexico, “integration with the United States and market access to the United States is priority No. 1,” mentioned Diego Marroquín, a fellow in the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. But “they can achieve that and at the same time, they can engage more with China,” he said, especially on issues that aren’t central to U.S. interests.

    In more sensitive areas, such as critical infrastructure and telecommunications, Mexico “will most likely accommodate U.S. demands,” Marroquín wrote this week.

    According to recent reports, chile has not imposed tariffs on Chinese goods, though it has seen tensions with China flare in other ways. This month, Chile and Belgium jointly challenged a Chinese bid to permanently host the secretariat of the fresh United Nations High Seas Treaty.

    The dispute over hosting rights is still unresolved, and Chilean President José Antonio Kast did not mention it in his bilateral meeting with Xi, according to multiple reports. The two countries announced a new economic cooperation road map without providing specifics. The partnership is potentially promising news for Chile as it experiences a recession.

    Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, meanwhile, walked away with a more concrete commitment from China: a $22.5 million pledge to help Peru deal with the fallout of El Niño. Both countries also celebrated an enhancement to their free trade deal that took effect this month, which officials said could help trade and investment rise by streamlining import- and export-related bureaucracy.

    Industry observers note that “Our meeting allows us to strengthen relations between Peru and China,” Fujimori wrote on social media after meeting with Xi. The Chinese readout stated that Fujimori praised the majority-Chinese-operated port in the Chancay, Peru—an investment that the Trump administration has criticized.

    In a recent development, fujimori, Kast, and Sheinbaum held additional bilateral meetings at APEC. Sheinbaum met with Trump, while all three Latin American presidents sat down with other Asian leaders, including those of Japan; Vietnam; the Philippines, with which Chile signed a free trade agreement; and Thailand, with which Peru did the same.

    Industry observers note that the meetings show that the three leaders hope to deepen ties not only with China but also more broadly with Asia. They are not alone in their neighborhood: Last weekend, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed the opening session of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines.

    These countries’ trade flows are beginning to reflect the presidential trips. To give one example, Mexico’s total goods traded with Japan between January and September of this year was 9 percent higher than over the same period in 2025, according to Mexican government statistics. With Thailand, trade grew by 50 percent, and with Malaysia, by 78 percent.

    According to recent reports, friday, Nov. 20: Fujimori meets Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Tokyo.

    Monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: Polish President Karol Nawrocki visits Argentina and Chile.

    Thursday, Dec. 3, to Friday, Dec. 4: Uruguay hosts the Mercosur leaders’ summit.

    Sources indicate that U.S. military deals. Less than a year after removing Venezuela’s president by force, the United States signed a military partnership with the country’s acting leaders on Wednesday. In Caracas to ink the deal, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called Venezuela a “compliant security partner” and mentioned the arrangement would allow both countries to better combat drug gangs.

    Former Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez ended Venezuelan military cooperation with the United States in 2005, and his successors in the chavismo movement have used their control over Venezuela’s military apparatus to cling to power and crush dissent.

    Industry observers note that rocío San Miguel, a top Venezuelan human rights advocate, told Union Radio that the U.S. partnership could be an opportunity to rein in Venezuela’s military, relegating it to its intended constitutional role.

    The Venezuela deal comes as U.S. military cooperation with neighboring Colombia appears to be falling short of Trump’s vision. The Latest York Times reported on Wednesday that Hegseth altered his travel plans to Colombia this week after the country’s government noted it lacked the congressional votes to greenlight U.S. military operations on its soil.

    Sources indicate that colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella wrote on social media afterward that he did not reject a specific initiative but added that any U.S. military cooperation must follow Colombian law.

    According to recent reports, shifting regional affinities. A gathering of Latin America scholars and policymakers in Rio de Janeiro last week highlighted the cross-border integration that is often excluded from headlines about the region. This newsletter writer attended the event, Conversatorio Latinoamericano.

    Sources indicate that one speaker flagged a recent University of Buenos Aires opinion survey about Argentines’ attitudes on geopolitics. Between 2025 and 2026, Brazil surpassed the United States to top respondents’ answers to two questions: “Which country do you think Argentina should have relations with?” and “Which country do you think Argentina should be like?”.

    The shift suggests that average Argentines don’t fully embrace President Javier Milei’s pro-Trump pivot—or his chilled relations with Brazil.

    Natalia Saltalamacchia Ziccardi of the Mexico Autonomous Institute of Technology noted that Brazil and Mexico are turning the page on years of distrust, experiencing a “springtime” of warming ties since around 2024. She cited increased high-level visits, coordination in response to Venezuela’s crisis, and shared support for a Chilean U.N. secretary-general candidate.

    These sympathies show that dividing the region into pro- and anti-Trump camps is an oversimplification.

    It has been revealed that chilean director Sebastián Lelio, winner of the best foreign language film award for A Fantastic Woman, poses in the press room during the 90th Academy Awards in Hollywood, California, on March 4, 2018.Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images.

    Recent findings suggest that chilean cinema pioneer. This month, Chileans are remembering star film director Sebastián Lelio, who died on Nov. 6 at the age of 52. Lelio got his start as part of a wave of indie Chilean filmmaking in the 2000s that focused on small-scale, interpersonal plotlines and was dubbed Novísimo Cine Chileno by critics.

    Lelio’s most beloved works include the 2013 film Gloria, which indicates the ups and downs of dating as a 58-year-old divorcée in the capital of Santiago, and the 2017 film A Fantastic Woman, which follows a transgender singer dealing with the logistics triggered by the death of her partner—and the prejudice that she faces from his conservative family.

    Recent findings suggest that A Fantastic Woman won Chile its first-ever Oscar for best foreign language film and helped pave the way for the passage of a 2018 trans rights law. Though Lelio worked across genres, La Tercera’s Gonzalo Valdivia wrote that he “found his natural habitat in portraits of female characters who don’t give in or apologize.”.

    Which Latin American country was the first to strike a free trade deal with China?

    The two countries signed the agreement in 2005.

    Industry observers note that panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro speaks during a press conference discussing electrification at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 18. Chris McGrath/Getty Images.

    The leaders of Antigua and Barbuda, the Bahamas, Barbados, Bolivia, Brazil, St. Lucia, and Venezuela all traveled to this year’s U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, known as COP31. The conference is due to wrap up on Friday.

    COP31 has moved the ball forward on some initiatives from last year’s U.N. climate summit, which Brazil hosted. For example, a planned investment fund that would pay countries to keep tropical forests intact has now raised more than $8 billion, thanks to a fresh pledge from Canada.

    Last week, Brazil published a framework for countries to create national prepares for transitioning away from fossil fuels, a topic that generated buzz at last year’s summit but was cut from the final agreement. Its potential inclusion in the COP31 agreement is still being haggled over.

    While Brazil has left a big mark on COP31, so too has a previous Latin American government: that of Colombian President Gustavo Petro, who departed in August. Unsatisfied with last year’s event, the Petro administration hosted a upcoming global conference in April that was devoted entirely to quitting fossil fuels, which will see a second edition next year in Tuvalu.

    In a recent development, A group of countries that was heavily involved in planning both conferences has also committed to creating a binding treaty on moving away from fossil fuels. Though Colombia has stayed quiet about the fossil fuel treaty initiative under de la Espriella, countries including Guatemala and Panama had joined it by the time that COP31 arrived.

    “We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia,” Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro noted at COP31.

    Many Latin American countries are currently led by right-wing leaders who have not styled themselves as climate champions. But they are nevertheless moving forward on an concern that has been proposed as a main outcome of COP31: electrification.

    According to recent reports, this year, Brazil is on track to more than double the number of electric vehicles, or EVs, sold since last year, while Mexico’s EV sales are up by more than 25 percent. Countries across the region are planning large-scale battery storage build-outs to support larger electric grids.

    The attractive price of green energy—and its insulation from global price shocks—is keeping the region’s green transition gradually moving forward.

    Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn.

    #42411. The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3946 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
    • At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
    • Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

    At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

    Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

    Yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

    In recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

    It has been revealed that at the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

    The success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

    International efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

    In the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

    Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

    Recent findings suggest that worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

    There is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

    A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France declared the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

    Sources indicate that simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

    Recent findings suggest that the integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

    Together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will quickly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

    Political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

    According to recent reports, in this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

    In a recent development, but these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

    It has been revealed that wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

    According to recent reports, war also creates upcoming dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

    In a recent development, finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to fresh waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

    The world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

    According to recent reports, but it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

    Spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

    In a recent development, from day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

    Recent findings suggest that deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

    Countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

    Industry observers note that investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

    Yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

    Reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

    Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

    Other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

    Industry observers note that the twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

    Sources indicate that all of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

    Sources indicate that strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

    The first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An revision to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly key, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The latest seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats at the moment occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

    According to recent reports, permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

    In a recent development, A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

    According to recent reports, another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral Latest START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

    Yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

    Technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

    Recent findings suggest that the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

    In a recent development, proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a new UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

    Halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

    It has been revealed that ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

    International financial institutions must be able to deliver financing quickly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

    This is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, rolled out with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

    A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that secure Solar Futures, a commercial solar contractor, will build a 313-kW solar power system at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, Virginia. Construction of the system is expected to start later this year at no cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year power purchase agreement with Secure Solar Futures.

    A total of 531 bifacial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, Texas, will be installed on the rooftop of the school, and the array is expected to offset 67% of the power used by the school annually. In its first year, the school’s solar system is projected to produce 421 MWh of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes.

    Recent findings suggest that under the PPA, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy and Secure Solar Futures will own, operate and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

    Industry observers note that preston Park Elementary School is expected to save $581,000 electricity costs over the term of the PPA. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s lifespan.

    News item from Secure Solar Futures.

    Latest Update: ICJ Finds Myanmar Committed Genocide. What Comes Next?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state.
    • Recent findings suggest that nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide.
    • According to recent reports, in August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

    Recent findings suggest that nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    According to recent reports, in August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

    It has been revealed that nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    Foreign Policy spoke with Tom Andrews, the former U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in Myanmar, a few hours after the ruling came down. He discussed the decision’s implications, including where justice lies for the world’s largest stateless population and how the ruling could affect similar genocide cases linked to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine.

    This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

    Foreign Policy: Earlier today, the ICJ found that Myanmar’s security forces had committed genocide against the country’s minority Rohingya Muslim community. For those who aren’t aware of the case, could you give a brief primer on the court’s findings?

    In a recent development, tom Andrews: They were very explicit in their findings. They talked about the thousands and thousands of people who were killed, the thousands of women who were raped, the more than 2,000 children who were killed, the hundreds of thousands of homes that were burned.

    I was in Bangladesh when people had arrived [in 2017], and I sat and talked to many people who had literally been running for their lives. And the stories they told me were just absolutely incredible. I mean the horror, the brutality, the systematic nature of the killing, of the rapes, of the torture, was just absolutely extraordinary. And, of course, more than 700,000 people escaped into Bangladesh; we know that 1.3 million are now in Bangladesh, in the largest refugee camp in the world.

    In a recent development, but what [the Rohingya] did was they pushed for justice and they pushed for accountability. And there were people who were victimized by this brutality, who came to the court, the International Court of Justice, and provided their own personal testimony, told their own stories in a private session, which I believe was a very powerful, powerful part of this whole process, where it allowed the judges to focus on the actual consequences, the human element of this.

    FP: This is the first time that the U.N.’s top court has found a nation directly responsible for genocide. What is the significance of that ruling?

    TA: History was made today. The standard for genocide is very, very high. And that is a reason why this is so remarkable. This is the first time it’s ever been made, because the standard not only includes the acts but also the intention behind those acts—that [the state] designed to harm a population in whole or in part.

    Sources indicate that but the question that it begs is, well, OK, now what? Now that we’ve established genocide, are there consequences for genocide, and what are they? And the court has ruled that the regime in Myanmar is responsible for providing relief and compensation for the victims.

    I believe that that needs to occur both within the United Nations and outside of the United Nations. Within the United Nations, I believe that the United Nations Security Council should take this up. I think they should pass a resolution. I think that these individuals who were responsible for this genocide should be criminally prosecuted, and so there should be a reference to the International Criminal Court for that criminal prosecution.

    I think it’s also notable for us to recognize that the killings that continue to go on are happening because the military junta—the generals and [junta leader] Min Aung Hlaing—has access to sophisticated weapons of war that it’s using to attack civilians. I think it’s really important that the international community do everything that it can to cut off that access to those weapons and those weapon materials, and the financing that’s being used to acquire those weapons and those weapon materials, so that we can stop that flow.

    In a recent development, another step that they can take is to reject this rehabilitation campaign that Min Aung Hlaing has been involved in now for the past few months. He’s been traveling to states in the region, to his neighbors, to ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] states. He’s been invited into these capitals, welcomed into these capitals. He’s been seeking to gain greater acceptance within ASEAN and the structure of ASEAN. And I think what’s really key is for those member states who have been moving in that direction of accepting or softening their relationship to Min Aung Hlaing and this genocidal regime to reverse those steps and that the regime be as isolated diplomatically as it deserves to be.

    FP: Do you think that the ruling will be enough, though, to actually push member states to take that next step and start to reverse the junta’s efforts to cast off its diplomatic pariah status?

    TA: I certainly hope so. I mean, this is unprecedented. This is a powerful, powerful moment for the world. I think it’s incredibly crucial for the world to respond to that finding in a responsible way and that member states and their citizens need to stand up and make their voices very, very clear and very strong that their government needs to do everything that it can to isolate this regime, weaken this regime, take away this regime’s capacity to continue to commit murder against its own people.

    Recent findings suggest that I mean, this is a moral imperative, and it is a call for everyone to make a moral stand for not only the Rohingya, not only for the people of Myanmar, but for justice and humanity around the world. Because the thing is, if we establish that there is no consequence for genocide, then we can be guaranteed that genocide is going to happen again. And it’s only by imposing consequences that we can begin to see justice prevail, not only in this case but in future cases.

    In a recent development, FP: What’s next for the Rohingya community themselves? The ICJ doesn’t have an enforcement mechanism, but could this case have a tangible impact on the future of that population?

    Industry observers note that TA: It can, and it should. First of all, the world has turned its back on the Rohingya. Support for the conditions in which they’re living, the refugee camps, has been declining. There have been increased difficulties in just being able to survive in these camps, in part, certainly, by the fact of the international community reversing commitments that it had made and support that it provided to people who are in these conditions for no fault of their own.

    According to recent reports, now, I think, with respect to reparations, the idea that the government of Myanmar—the current illegitimate regime of Myanmar—would accept the order of the court to provide compensation is, at best, a very, very remote possibility. In fact, I think that the chances of this happening are exactly zero. So, until there is a fresh regime that actually is legitimate and believes in justice and accountability and human rights, until that day happens, I think the world has to step forward, and I think there are options the world can take.

    For example, the United Nations can establish a reparations fund and a mechanism to manage that. The United States, for example, seized over a billion dollars in assets from this regime. And that billion dollars can be used as part of a compensation fund, and that can then be built upon with governments coming forward to provide additional resources so that there is some form of justice and compensation for those who were victimized by these attacks.

    FP: What is the view coming out of Myanmar right now? Is there talk of this case possibly leading to something like regime change?

    In a recent development, TA: I’ve heard reports of additional hate speech that’s beginning to be drummed up, some of the nationalists that have used hate speech against the Rohingya in the past, that they are beginning to once again generate that kind of hatred against the Rohingya. It’s a dangerous moment in the country.

    FP: Obviously, this case has an outsized impact on Myanmar’s future, but could this ruling affect similar cases at the ICJ on the conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine?

    According to recent reports, TA: It remains to be seen. The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations [Mike Waltz] posted a tweet in which—I’m paraphrasing here, but [he] accused the court of being poised to lower the standard for genocide, which could have an impact on future cases. And what’s happened is that the court was very explicit in saying that they used the current standard for genocide, including the standard of genocidal intent, in making this judgment. So, in fact, there was no lowering of the standard for genocide that some have accused the court of preparing to do.

    I think what’s vital is to focus on this case, to focus on this community and on people who were wronged, and to focus on our responsibility to them and to accountability and justice for them and to make sure that there is a consequence for genocide. So I’m hoping that we’re not distracted by what might happen in the future, that we’re focused on what’s happening right now.

    Industry observers note that I saw a report that a child is killed in these attacks every 29 hours in Myanmar now. So, yes, we need to stop the atrocities from continuing, but we need to focus on responsibility and accountability for these acts and these acts of genocide.

    Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp.
